reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .516 at the 98th percentile, and the barrel rate checks in at 13.6%, yet he's chasing 34.4% of pitches outside the zone — that's the tension in the profile. The raw power is elite-shelf, the contact quality backs it up, and an 11.4% walk rate suggests he's finding pitches to punish even while expanding; the 25.9% strikeout rate is the cost, and the projection absorbs it, arriving at a .948 OPS across 724 projected plate appearances with 46 home runs and 39 stolen bases. At 29.5 feet per second, he's among the fastest players in baseball, and that speed shows up in the stolen base line but also in everything the defense does for him. The thing to watch is whether that chase rate creeps higher as pitchers map him: if they find the outer edge and he follows, the strikeouts climb and the walk rate shrinks, and you're left with a different hitter than the one the xwOBA of .378 describes right now.

reports.name: Junior Caminero

Caminero's 92.8 mph average exit velocity sits in the 95th percentile, his hard-hit rate is nearly 50%, and a .498 xSLG tells you the power isn't outrunning his contact quality — the expected and actual profiles are aligned. The one structural tension is the fielding OAA at the 1st percentile, which means Tampa Bay either needs to find a positional solution or accept that his bat has to carry the full profile, and at .362 projected OBP with an 11.4% walk rate, it probably can. The question isn't whether he hits; it's whether he's a third baseman or a DH by 30.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: Thirty-four home runs with a 12.7% barrel rate is the shape of a real power hitter, and the .477 xSLG backs it up. What makes Stewart interesting is the gap between how he barrels the ball and how often he makes hard contact overall — the barrel rate sits in the 86th percentile while his Hard-Hit% lands near the middle of the league, which means he's finding the sweet spot without consistently elevating, a profile that tends to hold up as long as the chase rate (31.3%) doesn't creep further. At 22, a .271/.339/.477 projection across 702 plate appearances points to a middle-of-the-order corner with legitimate counting-stat upside. Sixteen stolen bases from a corner is a wrinkle most teams won't plan for.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact quality is legitimate, and the discipline numbers are the price you pay for it. Merrill's 91.5 mph average exit velocity and 49.0% hard-hit rate sit well above the median hitter's output, and the .493 xSLG explains where the projected 27 home runs come from. The problem is a 37.0% chase rate that ranks near the bottom of the league, and a 6.2% walk rate to match — at 23, he's selling the at-bat early and getting away with it because the ball jumps off the bat when he makes contact. If pitchers learn to live on the outer edges and he doesn't adjust, the chase rate becomes a ceiling rather than a footnote; if he holds his own, he's a 27-27 outfielder with real power in a full-season role.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact quality is almost unfair: a 53.7% hard-hit rate with a 92.9 mph average exit velocity puts him in rarefied air, and an xBA of .295 says the .285 projection is if anything a little conservative. What keeps this from being a straightforward superstar argument is the swing-and-miss, a 26.2% whiff rate that sits below the median despite a strikeout rate of 18.4% that looks fine on the surface, and a walk rate at roughly league average. The whole profile lives or dies on whether that contact quality keeps translating into results, and at 88th-percentile sprint speed with 37 projected stolen bases baked in, there's a second gear here that most hitters with this kind of raw thump don't carry. If the batted-ball profile holds, you're looking at a .355 OBP, 25 home runs, and that stolen base total from a guy who can play multiple positions — an everyday cornerstone, full stop.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact quality is elite and the chase rate is a liability, and those two facts are in direct tension. Walker's 92.5 mph average exit velocity and 13.2% barrel rate say power hitter; his 35.7% chase rate and 31.9% whiff rate say a pitcher who can expand the zone will find him. The .344 xwOBA suggests his current production is tracking close to his true talent level, and ValuCast sees the full-season output as .277/.335/.479 with 29 home runs and 21 steals across 667 plate appearances, which is a legitimate middle-of-the-order profile if the bat-to-ball issues don't deepen. The whole thing hinges on whether he makes enough contact against breaking balls away to keep pitchers from simply living there — if he does, this is a core piece; if he doesn't, the power and speed become decoration on a K% that sits at 25.5% alongside a walk rate that barely clears 7.6%.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Ryan Weathers
reports.published_report: The 3.59 ERA projection is doing Weathers a favor, and the Statcast profile explains why. His xERA sits at 4.28 with an xwOBA of .319, both in the bottom third of the league, and hitters are making hard contact at a 40.6% clip — his control is the one thing holding this together. At 6.7% walks with 25.2% strikeouts, the command-to-stuff ratio is genuinely inverted from what you want in a rotation piece: he limits free passes, but he isn't missing bats at a rate that punishes the contact he allows. If the control slips even modestly, there's no swing-and-miss floor to catch him, and a starter posting an xERA like that becomes a reliever-by-necessity story pretty quickly.

reports.name: Angel Martínez
reports.published_report:
The xwOBA is the problem. A 42.2% chase rate, bottom 4% of the league, is dragging his expected production well below what his contact and power numbers suggest he could be, and a 3.1% walk rate is the downstream consequence of that same aggression.

The bat-to-ball isn't the issue: a 20.4% whiff rate is clean enough, and the .255 xBA suggests he's making decent contact when he does connect. But chasing that relentlessly means pitchers never have to come to him, and the .304 xwOBA is the damage done. If he can't pull the chase rate toward something functional, the projection's .726 OPS over 407 PA is roughly the ceiling, not the floor, a guy with enough tools to keep a roster spot but not enough discipline to do more than that.

reports.name: Braylon Payne
reports.published_report: The ISO is the loudest thing in this profile. At 19 years old, posting .275 ISO across AA & A+ with 28 home runs and 25 stolen bases in 467 plate appearances, Braylon Payne is doing things most teenagers can't sniff at these levels. The translation is where it gets complicated: that raw power softens to .179 ISO in MLB-equivalent terms, which still clears the league average of .150, but the 29% strikeout rate across AA & A+ translates to 31.6% against big-league pitching, a rate that would put him well into negative contact territory at the highest level. If the strikeouts plateau here and don't travel up the ladder with him, you've got a lefty center fielder with real plus raw power and speed who could be a solid regular; if the swing-and-miss keeps climbing, the floor is a bench bat who shows up in spurts.

The power floor is low and the ceiling isn't much higher, with a 3.8% barrel rate, 35.4% hard-hit rate, and an xSLG that ranks near the bottom of the league, so the 12 projected home runs come from volume across 616 plate appearances, not authority. Rada has posted a 12% walk rate and made contact well enough to carry a .371 OBP across 571 plate appearances at AAA in 2026, and the discipline translates cleanly — his MLB-equivalent K% comes out at 20.7%, a tick below the major-league rate, with walks mapping to 10.6% where the average big-league hitter sits at 8.5%. The problem is the bat itself: .082 ISO at AAA, and the MLB-equivalent lands at .087 when the typical MLB hitter is at .150. The speed holds and the contact profile earns him enough plate appearances, he's a useful bench piece with real base-running value; if a major-league defense limits how often he reaches, there isn't enough bat to carry the lineup spot.

reports.name: Samuel Basallo
reports.published_report: A 12.6% barrel rate and 90.6 mph average exit velocity sitting in the top quarter of the league tells you the raw power is already there at 22. The problem is a 40.1% chase rate that ranks near the very bottom of qualified hitters, which drags his xBA all the way down to .237 even while his xSLG sits at .448. That split, elite contact quality on balls he hits paired with a zone-recognition problem that invites pitchers to expand endlessly, is what keeps the projection at .228/.297/.419 over 412 PA rather than something that looks like a middle-of-the-order catcher. If the chase rate comes down even modestly as he accumulates big-league reps, the power translates into an everyday backstop worth building around; if it doesn't, he's a DH-dependent regular whose bat plays below the threshold a catcher needs to carry.

reports.name: Jefferson Rojas
reports.published_report: The power profile here is legitimate across a real sample: 27 home runs and a .238 ISO across AAA & AA in 539 plate appearances, with that raw pop translating to a .174 MLB-equivalent ISO, comfortably above the .150 MLB mean. What complicates it is the walk rate. He draws walks at a 9% clip at the minor-league level, but the translation brings it to 7.9%, and his 20th-percentile walk ranking among his own peer pool tells you the contact and power are carrying what the discipline can't. He can sell you on the bat, .280/.346/.518 across AAA & AA, 91 strikeouts against 47 walks, 20 stolen bases, a K rate that translates below MLB average, but that 50th-percentile OBP relative to his pool is the tell: the contact and thump are doing most of the heavy lifting. This profile works as a bench or platoon bat; it becomes a floor if the power doesn't travel, because there isn't enough on-base skill to survive a rough stretch.

reports.name: Daniel Eagen
reports.published_report: The strikeout-to-walk profile is the argument: 157 strikeouts against 41 walks across 122 AA innings, a K-BB% that ranks 94th percentile among qualified pitchers and translates to 15.5% at the MLB level, where the average sits around 13.5%. That shape holds up at 11.6 K/9 and 3.0 BB/9 in the actual environment, and the ERA sitting at 4.7 with a 1.20 WHIP suggests the contact outcomes are lagging the command profile, not leading it. If the stuff translates into a big-league strike zone the way the peripherals suggest it might, Eagen becomes a reliable multi-inning or setup arm within a year or two; if the contact damage follows him up a level, the floor is depth.

reports.name: Cole Carrigg
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is quietly worrying: 87.9 mph average exit velocity, a 5.4% barrel rate, and a 35.7% chase rate all sit in the bottom third of the league, and the .311 xwOBA is the honest ceiling on his current contact quality. The projection at .265/.331/.459 is generous relative to what the underlying shape suggests, and it hinges entirely on whether Coors Field inflates the counting line enough to paper over the weak contact. What he does have is 28.8 ft/s sprint speed at the 86th percentile, and that shows up in the 11 projected steals and runs total. If the chase rate doesn't come down, you're looking at a fourth outfielder whose speed keeps him roster-relevant but whose bat never quite justifies a regular role.

reports.name: Zach Ehrhard
reports.published_report: The .401 OBP at AAA is doing real work here, but the translation is the part that deflates the profile. Across 621 plate appearances in AAA, Zach Ehrhard is hitting .290 with 93 walks, 20 home runs, and 27 stolen bases, a legitimately complete stat line for the level. The problem is that the ISO translates to .145 in an MLB equivalent, right at league average, and the K% lands at 22.1% while the MLB average sits at 22.0%, meaning the strikeout discipline that looks like a strength at AAA essentially disappears in translation. The walk rate holds at 12.5% translated, a number that would play in any big-league lineup, so there's a real skill underneath, but if the power doesn't add a tick in the jump, what you're left with is a high-OBP center fielder without the bat to carry a lineup spot.

reports.name: Braxton Ashcraft
reports.published_report: That 37.0% chase rate is doing real work here. Ashcraft gets hitters to expand at a clip that ranks among the most extreme in the league, and the 5.2% walk rate shows he's not buying it with free passes. The strikeout number sits at 25.9%, respectable but not overwhelming, which means the profile hinges on whether he can keep manufacturing soft contact when hitters don't chase. Hard-hit rate at 41.6% and average exit velo at 89.7 mph is where this gets interesting: those two are pulling in opposite directions, and the xERA of 3.42 suggests the contact management is holding well enough that the projection's 3.65 ERA and 166.3 innings feels like a reasonable landing spot for a mid-rotation starter who misses fewer bats than you'd expect from a guy throwing 97.3 mph.

reports.name: Kahlil Watson
reports.published_report:
The ceiling here is a bench bat, the floor is a depth piece, and the honest gap between them lives in one number: 28% strikeouts at AAA translating to 27.3% against MLB pitching.

That's not a swing-and-miss problem that disappears when he moves up, and it compresses everything else in the profile. The 57 walks and 19 home runs across 429 AAA plate appearances point to genuine discipline and pop, and the ISO translates to .165 at the MLB level, a tick above average, so the power has a real surface to land on. The 23 stolen bases add a dimension that makes the profile work harder at the margins.

If the strikeout rate softens even a little, you're talking about a useful left-handed bench piece who runs and hits for some power. If it holds at 27.3% in the bigs, the walks keep the OBP from cratering, but there isn't enough contact volume to push him past a platoon role.

reports.name: Zyhir Hope

The raw power translates to a .166 ISO against MLB pitching, which clears the MLB average of .150, but the 27% strikeout rate against that same competition is the thing the whole profile hangs on. reports.name: Brandon Lowe
reports.published_report: The power profile is legitimate and the contact profile is a problem. Lowe's 91.0 mph average exit velocity and 11.6% barrel rate both grade in the 76th percentile, and the projection has him at 33 home runs and a .483 SLG over 658 plate appearances — that's a genuine middle-of-the-order bat at second base. The catch is a 35.2% whiff rate that sits in the 4th percentile, paired with a 33.7% chase rate, and those two numbers together explain why his xBA lands at .238 despite all the raw thump. If pitchers continue to exploit that zone-discipline profile, the strikeout rate stays near its current 28.9% and the .260 AVG looks optimistic; if he makes even modest swing decisions, the power plays up and the .814 OPS projection becomes a floor.

reports.name: Spencer Miles
reports.published_report: The xERA is 2.97 and the barrel rate is 3.5%, and those two numbers basically tell you what Spencer Miles is: a contact manager who lives off soft contact rather than swing-and-miss. The 18.9% whiff rate and 27.6% chase rate are well below league average, so he is not fooling hitters out of the zone — he is just not giving them anything hard to hit when they do make contact, which is a thinner foundation than a strikeout-heavy profile but a real one. The whole thing hinges on whether that .268 xwOBA holds as a true skill or erodes when hitters sharpen their approach against him, because a 23.5% strikeout rate leaves no margin if contact quality creeps up. If it holds, he profiles as a legitimate high-leverage piece; if the contact management regresses, a 23.5% K rate in relief is not enough to fall back on.

The tension is that the contact is soft: 84.6 mph average exit velocity and a 3.9% barrel rate paint a profile that makes hard contact almost incidentally, which is why his xSLG sits at .356 even as his projected slash runs .284/.368/.437. He's getting to his counting stats, a projected 19 home runs and .805 OPS, by putting the ball in play relentlessly and walking at a 10.1% clip, not by punishing mistakes. reports.name: Noah Cameron
reports.published_report: The fastball sits 92.5 mph, which is a 19th-percentile reading among starters, and that's the whole tension in Cameron's profile. He makes it work through a 26.5% whiff rate and a 7.5% walk rate that plays well above the middle of the league, which is how a soft-thrower posts a 3.93 xERA that lines up neatly with his projected 3.86 ERA. The chase rate at 29.5% is the one thing to watch: he's not missing bats outside the zone at a high clip, so the whiffs are coming in the zone, and if hitters start sitting on his stuff, that contact quality could climb past what a 7.6% barrel rate suggests right now. If the command holds and hitters keep swinging where he wants, Cameron is a back-end starter who gives Kansas City a full workload and earns his rotation spot; if the below-average velocity gets exposed, there's a fifth starter who survives on margin, not ceiling.

reports.name: Nathan Flewelling
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the most interesting thing in this profile, and it might also be the most misleading part. At A+ across 486 plate appearances, Flewelling has drawn 71 walks against 132 strikeouts, a 15% walk rate that translates to roughly 11% at the MLB level, a figure meaningfully ahead of where MLB hitters sit on average, but his 27% strikeout rate at A+ becomes something closer to 30.5% when you run it through the level adjustment, and that's a hard number to build a catcher's career around. The .208 ISO at A+ is loud for a 19-year-old at that level, yet it softens to about .144 in MLB-equivalent terms, which lands right at the league-average power band, meaning the profile that looks like a power-and-patience bat in High-A looks more like a fringe regular once you translate it. Everything here hinges on whether the strikeout rate bends as he climbs; if it doesn't, what's left is a bench catcher with acceptable plate discipline and middling pop.

reports.name: Yandy Díaz
reports.published_report: The contact profile is genuinely unusual: a 14.9% whiff rate paired with a .283 xBA that grades out in the 93rd and 94th percentiles, respectively, meaning he makes hard, accurate contact at a rate almost no one in the league matches. The power reads as real contact quality rather than loft and launch — a 48.2% hard-hit rate with a barrel rate of just 7.2% tells you he's spraying line drives at 91.0 mph average exit velocity rather than selling out for lift. The ValuCast projection puts him at .294/.359/.453 across 702 plate appearances, which is a legitimate everyday number for a 35-year-old who can't run, and the whole profile hinges on whether the contact quality holds as he ages into a slower-twitch version of himself. If the bat-to-ball skill erodes, a 7.9% walk rate and 26.0 ft/s sprint speed don't leave much of a floor.

reports.name: Will Warren

Warren's 44.4% hard-hit rate and 90.9 mph average exit velocity sit at the very bottom of the leaderboard, and the .322 xwOBA with a 4.40 xERA is the truer picture of what hitters do when they connect. The saving grace is 2541 rpm on the fastball, elite spin that keeps strikeout and walk rates near average and presumably generates the weak swings when it works, but it isn't suppressing hard contact at a rate that makes a rotation spot comfortable. That gap between his ability to avoid walks and his inability to miss bats is what keeps a 128-inning body of work from adding up to more than a 4.8 ERA and a 1.3 WHIP. Depth arm ceiling, depth arm floor.

reports.name: Matt McLain
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is pulling in two directions at once. His chase rate sits at 26.5% and his walk rate at 10.0%, both pointing toward a disciplined hitter with a real feel for the zone, and his 9.6% barrel rate is legitimately above average contact quality when he does connect. But a 28.7% strikeout rate is doing serious damage to the output — the xBA lands at .216, which tells you the contact is sparse enough that even the barrels aren't saving the batting line, and the projection reflects exactly that: a .188/.279/.341 slash across 506 plate appearances. The whole profile hinges on whether he can cut the strikeout rate enough to let the walk discipline and above-average barrels actually surface in the counting stats; if that doesn't happen, the 16 home runs and 19 steals are buried inside a batting average that makes him hard to roster in a meaningful spot.

reports.name: Matthew Etzel
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the thing that exposes the ceiling problem. Across 493 plate appearances at AAA, Etzel is drawing walks at a 13% clip, which translates to an 11.2% MLB-equivalent rate while the league sits at 8.5%, and the .189 ISO at AAA suggests real enough pull-side thump to force pitchers into that zone. The trouble is the contact: a .243 average against a .296 BABIP means he isn't getting beaten on balls in play, he's just not hitting them hard enough often enough, and the MLB-equivalent strikeout rate of 25.3% will play worse against big-league stuff than it does now. If the power holds in translation, you've got a patient lefty bat who can work counts and punish mistakes off the bench; if the strikeouts creep and the ISO shrinks, what's left is a quadruple-A hitter who takes walks in an empty at-bat.

Across 47 innings at AA, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and when that command translates to an MLB context across AAA & AA, the walk rate holds — 2.7 BB/9, comfortably better than the MLB average, with a K-BB% that lands at 15.1%. The strikeout rate is the asterisk: his K/9 translates to 8.5, essentially matching what an average MLB arm produces, which means the profile lives or dies on whether the command stays elite enough to compensate. If it does, he's a useful depth piece who earns a rotation spot in a pinch; if the stuff doesn't miss enough bats against better competition, he settles into a bullpen role where the control still plays.

reports.name: Luke Hill

reports.name: Billy Amick
reports.published_report: The raw power is unmistakable and the strikeout hole is just as large. Across AAA & AA, Amick has hit 38 home runs with a .301 ISO in 520 plate appearances, but his 155 strikeouts translate to 30.6% at the MLB level, well above what the average big-league hitter sees, and his .224 average sits on a .239 BABIP that isn't leaving much room to hide. The walk rate is a genuine asset, translating to 9.8% at the MLB level, so there's a real on-base floor if the contact doesn't come, but first base is an unforgiving defensive home for a profile this reliant on power carrying the day. If the strikeout rate stays where it is, he's org depth with a loud highlight reel; if he finds even modest contact gains, the ISO translates to a second-division regular with real run-production value.

reports.name: Tsung-Che Cheng
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the best thing here, and it still might not be enough. Cheng has drawn 46 walks in 344 AAA plate appearances this season, a 13% clip that translates to 10.9% at the MLB level, where most hitters come in around 8.5%, but the power doesn't follow: his AAA ISO of .151 collapses to .132 in translation, a tick below the MLB mean of .150. The profile is a left-handed shortstop who controls the zone, runs a bit (10 stolen bases at AAA), and hits for almost no power once you adjust the environment, which leaves the whole thing hinging on whether the contact quality can creep up from a .241 AAA average or whether that .307 BABIP is already doing the heavy lifting. If it works, he's a bench piece who earns playing time through walks and speed; if the average bleeds further, what remains is organizational depth.

reports.name: Josh Kasevich
reports.published_report: The contact is elite and the power is nowhere. Kasevich's 12% strikeout rate at AAA translates to roughly 14.9% in an MLB context, comfortably below what most big-league hitters post, and his walk rate carries over almost flat at 8.7%, so the plate discipline profile is genuinely big-league ready. The problem is an .082 ISO at AAA that translates to .088 against MLB arms, roughly half what a typical MLB hitter produces, and four home runs across 563 AAA plate appearances don't leave much room to argue the power is hiding somewhere. If the bat-to-ball skill earns him a roster spot, the ceiling is a backup shortstop who makes contact and doesn't hurt you; if pitchers at the highest levels exploit the lack of impact, there isn't enough else to hold a job.
